name: Boab Prison Tree

location.address: Derby-Gibb River Road, adjacent to Myall's Bore, Derby, Western Australia 6728
location.neighbourhood: Derby Town Commonage, ~4-6km south of Derby township, on the road toward the Gibb River Road

access: Free, unrestricted public access per the National Trust register; a well-known roadside stop on Derby-Gibb River Road, protected by a post-and-wire fence to stop soil compaction and carving, with interpretive signage. No entry fee found in any source.
transport: No public transport; self-drive, roughly 4-6km south of Derby town on the road toward the Gibb River Road (sources give slightly different distances: WA state heritage register says 4km, other tourism sources say 6km).
verify_notes: Three independent tree-level coordinates cluster within a few hundred metres of each other (brief -17.347862/123.670163; Wikipedia infobox -17.3507/123.6699; National Trust register -17.35071/123.669941), so this is a genuine tree-level pin. Species confirmed twice directly: Wikipedia ('Adansonia gregorii') and the National Trust of Australia's own tree register (common name 'Boab Tree', botanical name 'Adansonia gregorii', other name 'Prison Tree'). AGE DISAGREEMENT, flagged rather than resolved: the National Trust register lists 'Age (approx) 500 yrs' as measured 02 Jul 1905 (so, per the register-pitfalls rule that a register age is the age at last measurement, that reads as roughly 500 years in 1905, i.e. approaching 620 today, though it is unclear whether 500 was ever more than a round contemporary guess). Separately, web search surfaced a 2024 peer-reviewed AMS radiocarbon dating paper (Patrut, Rakosy & von Reden, Studia UBB Chemia) specifically on this tree, reported in search summaries as finding a calibrated age around 1,185-1,250 years -- but the PDF could not be read directly in this pass (badly encoded/garbled extraction), so per the 'a search summary is a lead, never a source' rule that figure is NOT used as a verified fact here, only noted as an unconfirmed lead for a future pass with better PDF access. age_min is set conservatively to the one figure read on an actual fetched page (500), age_max left null rather than bridging to the unconfirmed radiocarbon number. Girth: no source states a girth or circumference directly; the National Trust register gives 'Diameter 4m' (measured same 1905 date) which converts via pi to a girth of roughly 1257cm -- recorded as girth_cm with the conversion noted, height given there as 8m (almost certainly canopy/measured trunk height at the hollow, not total tree height). IMPORTANT for the writer: the 'prison' story itself is now considered folklore. Historians Kristyn Harman and Elizabeth Grant, and separately anthropologist Kim Akerman, traced the 'prison tree' legend to a 1948 newspaper description of an artwork and concluded the story was transposed from a different, similarly-named boab tree at Wyndham (a separate WA town, not this one); there is no historical evidence Aboriginal prisoners were actually held in this specific tree's hollow. What IS well documented: anthropologist Herbert Basedow photographed and described the tree in 1916 as a 'live Boab used by the aborigines as hut and burial place', finding bleached human bones inside, suggesting genuine Aboriginal use as a dwelling/ossuary predating and separate from the colonial prison myth. The tree carries real cultural significance to the Nyikina and Warrwa people. It is WA state and municipal heritage listed (Shire of Derby-West Kimberley Municipal Inventory, Category 2, adopted 1995; WA Heritage Register), fenced for protection, and remains a living, actively-managed tourist landmark -- no evidence found of death or removal, condition listed 'Good' on the National Trust register. Single-tree-destination test: clearly passes -- one of the most recognisable individual trees in Australia and a standard stop for Kimberley/Gibb River Road tourists.
